articles.title: Five habits that stop most hacks

body.support:
Most hacks happen because of a weak password, or one tap on a fake link. Five habits stop most of it.

**1. Use a passphrase.** Four or more random words, like *purple kettle surfing wombat*. Don't use your name or birthday.

**2. One for each account.** Don't use the same one everywhere. Your **email** matters most.

**3. Turn on two-step login.** It sends a code to your phone when you log in. A thief can't get in without it.

**4. Spot phishing.** Fake messages:

- are **urgent**
- have a **link**
- ask for your **password** or a **code**.

Don't tap the link. Never give anyone a code.

**5. Update.** Install updates on your phone and apps. Check who can see your posts.

**Hacked?** Change your password. Turn on two-step login. Tell your bank if money is involved. Report it at **cyber.gov.au**.
body.core:
Most accounts aren't hacked by a genius in a hoodie. They're broken into because of a weak password, a reused password, or one tap on a fake link. Five habits stop most of it.

**1. Use a passphrase.** A **passphrase** is four or more random words, like *purple kettle surfing wombat*. It's long, so it's hard to crack, but easy for you to remember. Don't use your name, your pet, your footy team or your birthday.

**2. One per account.** If you use the same password everywhere, one leak opens everything. Your **email** matters most, because it can reset all your other passwords. A password manager can remember them all for you.

**3. Turn on two-step login.** **Two-step login** (also called **MFA**) asks for something extra, like a code sent to your phone or an app. Even if someone steals your password, they can't get in without it. Turn it on for email, banking, socials and myGov.

**4. Spot phishing.** **Phishing** messages pretend to be your bank, a delivery company, myGov or even a mate. Warning signs:

- it's **urgent** (*“Your account will be closed today!”*)
- it has a **link** to tap
- it asks for your **password**, **card details** or a **code**.

Don't tap the link. Go to the real app or website yourself. And **never** give anyone a login code. Real companies won't ask for it.

**5. Update and check.** **Updates** fix security holes, so install them. Check your **privacy settings** (who can see your posts and details) and your **recovery details** (the email and phone that can get you back in).

**If you get hacked:** change the password straight away, turn on two-step login, check your recovery details, and tell your bank if money's involved. You can report cybercrime at **cyber.gov.au**.
body.extend:
Most account compromises don't involve sophisticated attacks. They exploit weak or reused passwords, missing multi-factor authentication, unpatched software and phishing. Five habits address most of the risk.

**1. Passphrases.** A **passphrase** of four or more random words is long enough to resist guessing and cracking, yet memorable. Avoid personal details such as names, pets, teams or birthdays.

**2. Uniqueness.** Reusing a password means one breach compromises many accounts. Prioritise your **email**, which can reset everything else. A password manager makes unique passwords practical.

**3. Multi-factor authentication.** **Two-step login (MFA)** requires a second factor, such as an app code or security key. A stolen password alone is then insufficient. Enable it for email, banking, social media and myGov.

**4. Phishing.** **Phishing** messages impersonate trusted organisations or contacts. Indicators include urgency, an embedded link, and requests for credentials, card details or one-time codes. Navigate to the service independently rather than through the link, and never share a login code.

**5. Maintenance.** Install **updates** promptly, since they patch vulnerabilities. Review **privacy settings** and confirm your **recovery details** are current.

**If compromised:** change the password, enable MFA, verify recovery details, contact your bank if money is involved, and report cybercrime through **cyber.gov.au**.

caseStudies.title: A report every six minutes

body.support:
Australia has a government agency that tracks online crime. It's called the **ACSC**.

In **2024–25**, it got more than **84,700** reports of cybercrime. That's about **one every six minutes**.

For one person, the average cost was about **$33,000**.

Many people never report it. They feel embarrassed, or don't know where to go.

The ACSC says simple habits help a lot. Use passphrases. Turn on two-step login. Install updates.

You can report cybercrime at **cyber.gov.au**.
body.core:
Every year, the **Australian Signals Directorate's Australian Cyber Security Centre (ACSC)** publishes a report on cybercrime in Australia. It's the government agency that tracks online threats.

Its **Annual Cyber Threat Report 2024–25** found:

- The ACSC received more than **84,700** cybercrime reports in a year.
- That's about **one report every six minutes**.
- For individuals, the average reported cost of a cybercrime was about **$33,000**, up 8% on the year before.

Those are only the crimes people reported. Many people never report being scammed or hacked, because they're embarrassed or don't know where to go.

The good news: the ACSC says basic habits make a big difference. Use strong passphrases. Turn on two-step login. Install updates. Back up your important files. And be suspicious of messages that rush you.

You can report cybercrime, and get help to recover, at **cyber.gov.au**.
body.extend:
The **Australian Cyber Security Centre (ACSC)** is part of the Australian Signals Directorate. Each year, it publishes a report on the cyber threats facing Australia.

Its **Annual Cyber Threat Report 2024–25** found that the ACSC received more than **84,700** cybercrime reports in the year. That is roughly **one every six minutes**. For individuals, the average reported cost of a cybercrime rose 8%, to about **$33,000**.

These numbers only count crimes that people reported. Many cases never get reported. People feel embarrassed, don't know where to go, or think the loss is too small.

The ACSC's advice focuses on the basics: strong passphrases, two-step login, quick updates, regular backups, and caution with unexpected messages that rush you.

You can report cybercrime and get help to recover at **cyber.gov.au**.

teacher.overview: Students learn five digital security habits: passphrases, unique passwords (especially for email), two-step login (MFA), spotting phishing, and keeping devices updated with privacy and recovery settings checked. They annotate a phishing email, sort safe and risky habits, audit their own accounts (without writing passwords), and lock down one real account. The case study is the ASD's ACSC Annual Cyber Threat Report 2024–25: more than 84,700 cybercrime reports, about one every six minutes, with an average self-reported cost for individuals of about $33,000.
prep: Remind students never to write or share passwords; collect no personal details.
Check students have access to their own device and account; offer a practice account demonstration for those who don't.
Have cyber.gov.au and Scamwatch ready to show.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** four or more random words; long, so hard to crack, but easy to remember. Email can reset all your other passwords. Urgent, a link, asks for password, card details or a code (also: odd sender, no name, threats).

**Phishing email:** 1 fake sender (instagrarn); 2 urgent subject; 3 generic greeting; 4 threat; 5 dodgy link; 6 asks for a login code.

**Sort:** Footy2009 everywhere — risky; unique passphrase — safe; two-step login — safe; bank link in text — risky; ignoring updates — risky; sharing a code — risky.

**Case study:** cybercrime is constant and common; embarrassment or not knowing where to report; answers will vary.

realityCheck: **Privacy first.** Students must never write or show passwords; check settings screens only.
**Some students share devices or accounts.** Talk about why that's risky, kindly.
**MFA can lock people out.** Make sure recovery details are right before turning it on.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It's one of the most immediately useful lessons students get.
